heading: Remove Subtitles from Video – Hardcoded Caption Cleanup
intro:
Need to remove a subtitle that stays visible in every video frame? WatermarkGemini is preparing a dedicated workflow for burned-in captions in videos you own or may edit. The subtitle-cleanup processor is not live yet. If your captions can be turned off in the player, you may not need AI removal at all.

Concept illustrations for a planned workflow; not tested output. The dedicated tool is Coming Soon.

steps.title: Check Whether Subtitles Can Be Turned Off

faq.heading: Remove Subtitle from Video FAQs
faq.intro: Answers to the most common questions about use cases, formats, results, pricing, and safe editing.

items.question: How do I remove a subtitle from a video?
items.answer: First turn off subtitles in your video player. If they disappear, remove or disable the separate caption track when exporting. If the text remains in every frame, it is hardcoded and needs source-project editing or a tested video-repair workflow.

items.question: Can I remove subtitles from a video online for free?
items.answer: The dedicated WatermarkGemini subtitle remover is Coming Soon, so a free online processing allowance is not confirmed. For soft subtitles, removing the track or switching captions off may be free in your existing player or editor.

items.question: What are hardcoded or burned-in subtitles?
items.answer: Hardcoded subtitles are rendered into the video pixels. They remain visible even if you disable captions in the player. Removing them may require rebuilding the covered parts of the frame.

items.question: What is the difference between soft and hard subtitles?
items.answer: Soft subtitles are separate tracks or files that can usually be switched off, detached or omitted from an export. Hard subtitles are part of the image and require original-project access, cropping, or image-based cleanup.

items.question: Can I remove subtitles from an MP4 video?
items.answer: An MP4 can contain either a separate subtitle track or burned-in captions. Inspect which type you have before choosing a method. The WatermarkGemini dedicated hardcoded-caption workflow is not available for processing yet.

items.question: Can I remove subtitles without cropping the video?
items.answer: For a soft track, disabling it leaves the video picture unchanged. For burned-in captions, targeted repair may preserve the frame, but the area under the text must be estimated and could show artifacts.

items.question: Will subtitle removal damage faces or moving backgrounds?
items.answer: It can. Captions placed over faces, hands, complex textures, or camera movement are harder to repair without blur or flicker. Always inspect the whole clip, not a single before-and-after frame.

items.question: Does subtitle removal work in different languages?
items.answer: Once text is burned into the pixels, the challenge is visual restoration rather than just the language. Multilingual and two-line captions should be tested separately; no language support claim is verified for this Coming Soon editor.

items.question: Can I remove captions or karaoke text that change every frame?
items.answer: Animated captions and karaoke highlights require more demanding frame-by-frame tracking and repairs. This capability has not been established for the current product; the original editing project remains the preferred option.

items.question: Can I use this tool to remove someone else’s subtitles?
items.answer: Only edit video you created, licensed, or have explicit permission to modify. Captions may be part of licensed content or important accessibility information; preserve an accessible caption option where appropriate.

items.question: When will the subtitle remover be available?
items.answer: The page currently says Coming Soon and does not give a confirmed launch date. The final feature list, accepted formats and any processing charges should be published when testing is complete.

features.heading: What the Planned Subtitle Removal Workflow Will Address
features.intro: Start by identifying subtitle type; only burned-in captions call for picture repair.

items.heading: Understand Hardcoded vs. Soft Subtitles First
items.description: Not every subtitle needs pixel removal. Soft subtitles are a selectable track or external caption file, so they can often be disabled in the player or removed when re-exporting. Hardcoded or burned-in captions are already part of the video image and may require AI-assisted repair. This planned page focuses on the second case and makes that distinction clear before asking users to upload anything.
items.imageAlt: Understand Hardcoded vs. Soft Subtitles First — same camera frame and matched target region.

items.heading: Target the Subtitle Band Without Cropping
items.description: The intended workflow will focus on a subtitle region instead of cutting away the bottom of the entire frame. This matters for interviews, tutorials, and vertical content where a crop can hide hands, products or action. The eventual product must be tested on lines in different positions, sizes and languages before claiming broad support. Until launch, retain the original project whenever possible.
items.imageAlt: Target the Subtitle Band Without Cropping — same camera frame and matched target region.

items.heading: Plan for Consistent Frame-by-Frame Cleanup
items.description: A single still can look clean even when an entire clip flickers. Burned-in subtitles change over time, while backgrounds and subjects move behind the text. A release-ready subtitle remover should be evaluated across scene cuts, moving faces, lower-thirds, dual-language captions and overlapping text. These are QA requirements, not proven abilities of the current Coming Soon page.
items.imageAlt: Plan for Consistent Frame-by-Frame Cleanup — same camera frame and matched target region.

items.heading: Keep Processing Rules and Availability Transparent
items.description: The dedicated subtitle processor is under development. Do not advertise free MP4 processing, supported languages, fixed output quality, or unlimited duration before the real editor has been tested. Once ready, state the accepted file types, limits, processing cost, sign-in rules, and deletion policy beside the uploader. For now, readers can use the page to understand which subtitle type they have and their safest editing options.
